# Abstract (500 words excluding titles, references)

Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being leveraged for the
annotation of large corpora [e.g. @yu2024]. In an early evaluation of
such an application, @morin2025 presented "a replicable method for
automating grammatical annotation" using Anthropic's model Claude 3.5
Sonnet [@morin2025: 4]. Their annotation pipeline consisted of a complex
"conversation" with the model over several iterative phases of training
and testing. They were able to achieve an accuracy of 93% compared to the gold standard provided by a human annotator [@morin2025: 6], and point out that they put forward a replicable annotation method that can be used for other constructions in different languages [@morin2025: 7].

We aimed to repeat @morin2025's "replicable method" as closely as
possible, using the same data, albeit with two open LLMs, Mistral Small
3.2 24B Instruct [@mistralai2026] and OpenAI GPT OSS 120B [@openai2026]. While the smaller Mistral model did not perform as well on the task (accuracy of 67%), the open GPT model yielded very similar results (accuracy of 94%).
Whilst the authors published their data and a full transcript of their
"conversation" with the model [@morin2024], we found that essential
information to independently replicate the study (e.g., whether the web
interface or an API was used, analysis code, etc.) was missing - forcing
us to make some educated guesses as to the exact procedure. Our results
suggest that, as of early 2026, large commercial LLMs may not be necessary
to complete this kind of linguistic task.

Next, we tested the need for such an extensive 'in-conversation'
training process. To this end, we conducted a second, extended
replication applying a much simpler few-shot training approach the
best-performing open LLM from our first replication. Our results suggest
that the training process need not be as elaborate as in @morin2025 to
accomplish similarly high accuracy rates.

Finally, we replicated the annotation study using a fine-tuned
DistilBERT model (<!--# Add ref: the paper or the transformers library?? -->). Although this encoder-only
transformer is considerably smaller than even a small generative LLM, it
achieved a performance comparable to that of a small LLM (approximately
on par with the 24B Mistral model used in our first replication). These
findings indicate that task-specific supervised models may provide a
competitive and more computationally efficient alternative to generative
LLMs.

Our results have important implications for the replicability of
corpus-linguistic research involving LLMs. We argue that, when choosing
a method, issues around model accessibility, data leakage, and carbon
footprint can and should be taken into consideration.
